title: The Quiet Room Beside the Gym
passage:
When Kenta's school rebuilt its gym, one small room was left without a clear purpose. It had once stored sports equipment, but new storage cabinets made it unnecessary. Some teachers suggested turning it into another meeting room. Others wanted to use it for club supplies. Before deciding, the student council asked students what kind of space they felt the school was missing.

The answers surprised them. Many students did not ask for another place to study or meet friends. Instead, they wanted somewhere quiet to sit for a short time. The library was quiet, but students were expected to read or study there. The nurse's office was available when someone felt sick, but students did not want to visit it simply because they were tired or overwhelmed. Several students said that during busy school days, they sometimes needed ten minutes without conversation.

The council proposed a trial. The empty room would become a quiet room for one month. It would have six chairs, no music, and no group conversations. Students could enter during lunch or after school and stay for up to fifteen minutes if others were waiting. A teacher would check the room regularly, but students would not need permission to use it.

During the first week, only a few students entered. Some thought the room was meant only for students with serious problems. The council added a sign saying, ‘This room is for anyone who wants a short quiet break.’ Use increased quickly. Students came after tests, before club practice, or simply when the cafeteria felt too noisy.

One concern appeared after two weeks. A few students began using the room for long private conversations. That made others uncomfortable. The council did not add many rules. They simply clarified that the room was for quiet individual use and suggested other spaces for talking. After that, conflicts decreased.

At the end of the month, the council collected feedback. Most users said the room was useful not because it solved a large problem, but because it gave them a small choice during the day. Teachers also noticed that students who used the room usually returned to class or club activities after a short break. The school decided to keep the space. Kenta learned that useful facilities do not always need complicated equipment. Sometimes the value of a place comes from what it allows people not to do for a while: not talk, not perform, and not respond to anyone.
translation:
ケンタの学校で体育館を改修した際、小さな部屋が一つ余りました。以前は運動用具の倉庫でしたが、新しい収納棚ができたため不要になったのです。会議室にする案や部活動用品の保管場所にする案が出ましたが、生徒会はまず、生徒たちが学校にどんな場所が足りないと感じているかを尋ねました。

意外にも、多くの生徒が求めたのは勉強や友人との交流の場所ではなく、短時間静かに過ごせる場所でした。図書館では読書や学習をする雰囲気があり、保健室は体調が悪いときの場所です。忙しい学校生活の中で、ただ十分快く話さずに過ごしたいことがあるという声が多くありました。

そこで一か月間、空き部屋を『静かな部屋』として試すことになりました。椅子を六脚置き、音楽やグループでの会話は禁止しました。昼休みや放課後に入り、混んでいれば一人十五分まで利用できます。先生が定期的に確認しますが、利用許可は必要ありません。

最初は利用者が少なく、深刻な悩みがある人だけの部屋だと思われていました。そこで『短い静かな休憩をしたい人なら誰でも使えます』という案内を出すと、利用が増えました。テスト後、部活前、食堂が騒がしく感じるときなどに使われました。

二週間ほどすると、長い個人的な会話に使う生徒が現れ、他の利用者が困ることがありました。生徒会は細かな規則を増やすのではなく、ここは一人で静かに過ごすための場所だと改めて明確にし、会話には別の場所を案内しました。その後、問題は減りました。

一か月後の調査では、多くの生徒が『大きな問題を解決するからではなく、一日の途中に小さな選択肢があることがよい』と答えました。先生たちも、短い休憩の後には授業や部活へ戻っていることに気づきました。学校は部屋を残すことにしました。ケンタは、役立つ施設には必ずしも複雑な設備が必要ではなく、ときには『話さない、頑張らない、誰かに応えない』時間を許すこと自体に価値があると学びました。

title: The Market's Last Hour
passage:
A weekend farmers' market in Hoshi Town was busiest between nine and eleven in the morning. By noon, many shoppers had left, but several vegetable sellers still had boxes of produce that had not been sold. Some items could be taken home and sold the next day, but soft vegetables and ripe fruit often lost quality quickly. Sellers disliked throwing food away, yet cutting prices too early could reduce their income.

A group of university students studying food waste asked whether the final hour of the market could work differently. They first observed the market for three weekends. They found that sellers already lowered some prices near closing time, but each stall did it differently. Shoppers did not know when discounts would begin, and some waited until the last minute hoping for very low prices. This sometimes created frustration.

The students suggested a simple shared system. During the final forty-five minutes, stalls could place a blue card beside items they wanted to sell quickly. The card did not require a certain discount. It only meant that the seller was open to a lower price or a larger bundle. Shoppers were asked not to bargain at stalls without the card.

At first, several sellers worried that customers would ignore full-price items all morning and wait for blue cards. The students therefore tested the system only on products that sellers selected near closing time. They also displayed information explaining that the goal was to reduce waste, not guarantee cheap food.

After four weeks, the amount of unsold produce taken away from the market had fallen. Sellers said they liked being able to choose which products entered the system. Shoppers said the blue cards made the final hour easier to understand. One unexpected result was that some customers began buying imperfect vegetables even before closing because the project had made them think more about waste.

The system did not remove all waste. Weather still affected attendance, and some food remained unsold. However, the market learned that a small piece of shared information could improve decisions for both sides. Before the experiment, every seller and shopper had been guessing what the other side might do. The blue card did not set a price or force anyone to buy. It simply made one intention visible. In a place where many small choices happen quickly, that little bit of clarity was enough to change behavior.
translation:
星町の週末農産物市場は、午前九時から十一時ごろが最も混みます。正午になると客は減りますが、売れ残った野菜や果物を抱える店もありました。翌日に持ち越せるものもありますが、柔らかい野菜や熟した果物は品質が落ちやすく、捨てることもありました。しかし早い時間から値下げすると収入が減るため、店側には難しい問題でした。

食品ロスを研究する大学生グループは、閉店前の一時間を別の形で運用できないか考えました。三週にわたり観察すると、実際には多くの店が終了間際に値下げしていましたが、方法がばらばらでした。客はいつ安くなるか分からず、さらに大きな値下げを期待して最後まで待つ人もおり、不満が生まれることもありました。

学生たちは、終了四十五分前から、早く売りたい商品に青いカードを置く共通方式を提案しました。カードは特定の割引率を意味しません。値下げやまとめ売りに応じる意思があることだけを示します。カードのない店では値引き交渉をしないよう客にも説明しました。

店側には『朝から値下げを待つ客が増えるのではないか』という心配もありました。そこで、閉店近くになってから店主自身が選んだ商品だけにカードを付けることにし、目的は安売りではなく廃棄削減だと掲示しました。

四週間後、持ち帰る売れ残りは減りました。店側は対象商品を自分で選べる点を評価し、客も閉店前の仕組みが分かりやすくなったと感じました。さらに、食品ロスへの関心が高まり、閉店前でなくても形の悪い野菜を買う人が増えるという予想外の変化もありました。

すべての廃棄がなくなったわけではありません。天候で客数が変わり、売れ残る日もあります。それでも、市場は小さな情報共有が売る側と買う側の判断を改善すると学びました。青いカードは価格を決めるものでも購入を強制するものでもありません。ただ『早く売りたい』という意思を見えるようにしただけです。その小さな分かりやすさが、多くの判断が短時間に行われる市場では十分な効果を持ったのです。

title: A Classroom Without a Front
passage:
Room 3B had been arranged in the same way for years. Thirty desks faced the whiteboard, and the teacher's desk stood in front. The arrangement worked well for lectures, but the class increasingly used discussions, presentations, and group projects. Moving heavy desks several times a day took time, so teachers often kept the traditional layout even when it did not match the activity.

During a school improvement project, students were asked to suggest changes that would cost almost nothing. A student named Haruka proposed marking several desk positions on the floor. One set of small marks would show the usual lecture layout. Another would show groups of four. A third would create a large open square for discussion. The class could then move desks quickly without arguing about where they should go.

The idea seemed almost too simple, but the teacher allowed a two-week test. Students used removable tape in three different colors. On the first day, changing from lecture rows to groups took more than five minutes because students had to understand the system. By the fourth day, the same change took less than two minutes.

A different problem appeared during square discussions. Students at the corners had difficulty seeing everyone, and two desks blocked the door. Haruka's group adjusted the marks. They also realized that not every lesson needed a special layout. Sometimes changing the room created more trouble than benefit. The marks were most useful when the teacher clearly knew why the arrangement should change.

After a month, two other classes copied the idea. Each adapted the patterns to its room rather than using exactly the same design. One room had a central pillar, while another had fewer desks. The important part was not the colored tape itself but the idea of making repeated changes easier.

Haruka had originally thought of classroom design as choosing where furniture should stay. The project changed her view. A good room can also be designed for movement. If people often need to switch between different kinds of work, then the space should help them change quickly. The classroom became more useful not because it received new furniture, but because students created a simple system for using the furniture they already had in several ways.
translation:
3B教室は長年、三十台の机が黒板方向を向き、前に教卓がある同じ配置でした。講義には向いていますが、最近は話し合いや発表、グループ活動が増えています。重い机を一日に何度も動かすのは大変なので、活動に合わなくても従来の配置のまま授業をすることがよくありました。

学校改善活動で『ほとんど費用をかけずにできる工夫』を考えることになり、ハルカは床に机の位置を示す印を付ける案を出しました。一つは普通の列、もう一つは四人グループ、さらに話し合い用の大きな四角形です。どこへ動かすか毎回相談せず、すぐ配置を変えられるようにする狙いでした。

二週間試すことになり、色の違うはがせるテープを使いました。初日は仕組みを理解するのに時間がかかり、列からグループへ変えるだけで五分以上必要でした。しかし四日目には二分未満で変更できるようになりました。

一方、四角形の配置では角の生徒が全員を見にくく、扉をふさぐ机もありました。そこで印を修正しました。また、すべての授業で配置変更が必要なわけではなく、目的が明確なときにこそ役立つことも分かりました。

一か月後には他の二クラスも取り入れましたが、中央に柱がある教室や机数が少ない教室など、それぞれに合わせて形を変えました。大切なのは色テープそのものではなく、繰り返す変更を簡単にする考え方でした。

ハルカは以前、教室設計とは家具をどこに置いておくか決めることだと思っていました。しかしこの経験から、動かしやすさも設計できると知りました。異なる活動へ頻繁に切り替えるなら、その変化を助ける空間にすればよいのです。新しい家具を買ったのではなく、今ある家具を複数の方法で使える仕組みを作ったことで、教室はより使いやすくなりました。

title: The Bus Stop with Two Clocks
passage:
Near the university hospital, a bus stop served two routes. Route A was run by the city, while Route B was operated by a private company. Each company had installed its own digital display. One screen showed the scheduled departure time. The other showed an estimated number of minutes until the bus arrived. Passengers often assumed the two screens were giving the same kind of information.

This caused confusion when buses were delayed. A passenger might see ‘10:20’ on one screen and ‘8 minutes’ on the other at 10:15. Some thought one of the displays was broken. Others waited for the wrong bus because they did not notice that the systems worked differently. Hospital staff heard frequent questions from visitors, especially older people and those unfamiliar with the area.

A transportation class at the university studied the stop as a small communication problem. The students interviewed passengers and discovered that most could understand both systems when they were explained separately. The difficulty came from placing different types of information side by side without clear labels.

The class suggested adding two large headings: ‘Scheduled Time’ and ‘Live Estimate.’ They also proposed using the same route colors on both signs and on a printed map. The companies agreed to test the labels, but they could not immediately replace their digital systems because the equipment came from different suppliers.

For three weeks, students observed the stop before and after the change. Questions to hospital staff decreased. More passengers looked from the live estimate to the scheduled time and understood that a delay was occurring. Some still preferred one system over the other, but fewer assumed that the displays were contradictory.

The project showed that more information is not always clearer information. Both displays had been accurate in their own way, yet the combination confused people because the relationship between them was invisible. The solution did not require better sensors or a new app. It required a few words that told people what kind of information they were seeing. The students learned that when systems are placed together, designers must explain not only each part, but also how the parts differ.
translation:
大学病院の近くに、二つの路線が利用するバス停がありました。A路線は市営、B路線は民間会社が運行しており、それぞれが別のデジタル表示を設置していました。一方は『予定時刻』、もう一方は『到着まで何分か』を表示していましたが、利用者は同じ種類の情報だと思うことがありました。

遅延が起きると混乱が増えました。たとえば10時15分に、一方に『10:20』、もう一方に『あと8分』と出ると、どちらかが故障していると思う人もいました。仕組みの違いに気づかず、別のバスを待つ人もいました。病院職員には、特に地域に慣れていない人や高齢者からの質問がよく寄せられていました。

大学の交通を学ぶ授業でこのバス停を調べると、二つの仕組みを別々に説明すれば多くの人が理解できることが分かりました。問題は、異なる種類の情報が明確な説明なしに並んでいることでした。

そこで学生は『予定時刻』『現在の到着予測』という大きな見出しを付け、路線色も表示と地図で統一するよう提案しました。設備自体は会社ごとに異なるためすぐ交換できませんでしたが、ラベルは試すことができました。

三週間観察すると、病院職員への質問は減り、利用者も予定時刻と到着予測を見比べて遅延を理解するようになりました。どちらの表示が好みかは人によって違いましたが、矛盾していると思う人は減りました。

この計画から、情報は多ければ多いほど分かりやすいわけではないと分かります。どちらの表示もそれぞれ正確でしたが、違いが説明されていなかったため混乱を生みました。必要だったのは新しいセンサーやアプリではなく、『何を示しているか』を伝える数語でした。複数の仕組みを並べるときには、それぞれの説明だけでなく、互いにどう違うかも示す必要があるのです。

title: The River After the Festival
passage:
Every summer, a riverside park hosted a food and music festival. Thousands of people came during the weekend, and local shops valued the event because it brought visitors to the town. On Monday morning, however, volunteers often found plastic cups, food containers, and paper decorations near the river. Cleanup teams worked for hours, but some light trash had already blown into the water.

The organizers first responded by adding more trash bins. The next year, they placed twice as many bins around the park. Cleanup became slightly easier, but litter near the river did not decrease much. Volunteers noticed that the bins closest to food stalls filled quickly, while bins only fifty meters away remained almost empty. People tended to use the nearest visible bin, especially when they were carrying food.

Before the following festival, organizers changed their approach. Instead of simply increasing the number of bins again, they mapped where people walked and where trash was usually found. They created small waste stations at the busiest crossing points and placed signs above head height so the stations could be seen through crowds. Each station had separate openings for bottles, burnable waste, and food containers.

They also changed the final hour of the festival. Staff members visited food stalls before closing and asked sellers to remove loose signs, empty boxes, and packaging that could blow away. Volunteers began a light cleanup while visitors were still present instead of waiting until everyone had left.

After the festival, the total amount of waste was similar to the previous year because visitor numbers were also similar. Yet much less trash was found near the water, and cleanup finished earlier. The improvement did not come from asking visitors to become more responsible. Most people had already intended to throw things away properly. The problem was that crowded conditions made the correct action less convenient.

The organizers learned to separate two questions: how much waste an event produces and where that waste ends up. Reducing the total amount would require changes in packaging and sales. Preventing litter required a different strategy based on movement, visibility, and timing. By understanding the exact problem they wanted to solve, they found a more effective solution than simply buying more bins.
translation:
毎夏、川沿いの公園では食べ物と音楽の祭りが開かれ、週末には何千人もの人が訪れます。町の店にとっては大切なイベントですが、月曜日の朝には川の近くにプラスチックカップ、食品容器、紙飾りなどが多く残りました。清掃に何時間もかかり、軽いごみの一部はすでに川へ飛んでいました。

主催者は最初、ごみ箱を増やしました。翌年は数を二倍にしましたが、川辺の散乱ごみはあまり減りませんでした。食べ物の店の近くのごみ箱はすぐ満杯になる一方、五十メートル離れたものはほとんど空いていました。食べ物を持つ人は、近くに見えるごみ箱を使う傾向が強かったのです。

そこで次の年には、人の歩く経路とごみが見つかる場所を地図にしました。人が交差する場所に回収ステーションを置き、混雑していても見えるよう高い位置に案内を出しました。ステーションはボトル、燃えるごみ、食品容器を分けられるようにしました。

祭りの最後の一時間の運用も変えました。閉店前に店へ声をかけ、風で飛びそうな看板、空箱、包装を片付けてもらいました。また、客が全員帰ってからではなく、まだ会場に人がいるうちから軽い清掃を始めました。

来場者数がほぼ同じだったため、ごみの総量も大きくは変わりませんでした。しかし川の近くで見つかるごみはかなり減り、清掃も早く終わりました。改善した理由は、来場者に『もっと責任を持って』と求めたからではありません。多くの人はもともと正しく捨てるつもりでした。ただ混雑の中では正しい行動がしにくかったのです。

主催者は『ごみをどれだけ出すか』と『そのごみがどこへ行くか』は別の問題だと学びました。総量削減には包装や販売方法の変更が必要ですが、散乱防止には人の動き、見つけやすさ、時間帯を考える必要があります。解決したい問題を正確に分けて考えたことで、単にごみ箱を増やすより効果的な方法が見つかりました。

title: The Lunch Line Experiment
passage:
At Seiwa School, the lunch line often stretched across the cafeteria. Students complained that they spent too much of their break waiting. The kitchen staff worked quickly, and adding another serving counter would have required expensive construction. A teacher suggested that the problem might not be the speed of serving itself.

For several days, a student team timed different parts of the line. They discovered that most meals were handed over in less than twenty seconds. The larger delays happened earlier, where students stopped to choose between two side dishes and then searched for forks, spoons, or chopsticks. People behind them could not move forward even when food was ready.

The team tested a new arrangement. A menu board with photos was placed outside the cafeteria so students could choose a side dish before joining the line. Utensils were moved to a separate table after the serving counter. This meant students who needed time to decide or search for something would not block the food station.

During the first two days, the new arrangement caused different confusion. Some students forgot to take utensils because they were used to picking them up earlier. Others changed their side-dish choice at the counter, slowing the line again. The team added arrows on the floor and placed a small reminder sign beside the trays.

After one week, the average waiting time during the busiest period had dropped by about three minutes. That sounded small, but lunch break was only forty minutes, so students noticed the difference. Kitchen staff also said the line felt calmer even though they were serving the same number of meals.

The experiment changed how the student team thought about waiting. A long line does not always mean that the main service is too slow. Sometimes the delay is caused by several small decisions happening in the same narrow place. By moving choices and simple tasks to different points, the school improved the flow without making anyone work faster. The lesson was useful beyond the cafeteria: when many people share a process, it can be better to redesign the sequence than to demand more speed from the people inside it.
translation:
清和中学校では昼食時の列が食堂の中を長く伸び、生徒たちは休み時間の多くを待ち時間に使っていると不満を感じていました。調理スタッフは十分速く働いており、配膳台を増やすには大きな工事費が必要でした。そこで先生の一人が、問題は配膳速度そのものではないかもしれないと考えました。

生徒チームが数日間、列の各部分にかかる時間を測ると、食事を受け取る時間はほとんど二十秒未満でした。大きな遅れはその前にありました。二種類のおかずから選ぶ場所や、フォーク、スプーン、箸を探す場所で人が止まり、後ろの人も進めなくなっていたのです。

そこで、食堂の外に写真付きメニューを置き、列に入る前におかずを選べるようにしました。食器類は配膳台の後ろにある別のテーブルへ移しました。判断や物探しに時間がかかる人が、食べ物を受け取る場所をふさがないようにしたのです。

最初の二日は別の混乱が起きました。以前の場所に慣れていたため、食器を取り忘れる人や、配膳台で選択を変える人がいました。床に矢印を付け、トレー横に小さな注意表示を置くと改善しました。

一週間後、最も混む時間帯の平均待ち時間は約三分短くなりました。昼休みは四十分しかないため、生徒にとって三分は十分感じられる差でした。調理スタッフも、同じ人数へ同じ速度で配膳しているのに列が落ち着いたと感じました。

この実験から、長い列があるからといって主なサービスが遅いとは限らないことが分かりました。同じ狭い場所で複数の小さな判断をさせることが遅れの原因になる場合があります。作業を違う場所へ分け、順番を設計し直すことで、誰かにさらに速く働くよう求めなくても流れを改善できたのです。

title: The Empty Seats on the Third Floor
passage:
A city learning center had study rooms on three floors. Every evening, students lined up for seats on the first floor, while many desks on the third floor remained empty. Staff assumed students simply preferred being near the entrance. Because the first floor was crowded, they considered adding more desks there.

Before buying furniture, the center surveyed users. Some did prefer the entrance, but many gave another reason: they did not know whether seats were available upstairs. Walking to the third floor and finding it full felt like a waste of time, so they joined the visible line downstairs instead. In fact, the third floor was rarely full.

The center could not afford an electronic seat-counting system. A staff member suggested a low-cost alternative. Every thirty minutes, a worker already making safety rounds would record roughly how many desks were free on each floor. A small board near the entrance would show ‘many seats,’ ‘some seats,’ or ‘almost full.’ The information would not be exact, but it would be recent enough to guide people.

The first week showed an unexpected problem. Users treated the board as if it were perfectly accurate. When ‘many seats’ was displayed but a large group had just gone upstairs, some students complained. Staff changed the wording to ‘recent estimate’ and added the time of the last check. That small change helped people understand that the information could change.

Within a month, the first-floor line became shorter, especially on weekday evenings. More students used the third floor, and the center no longer planned to buy extra desks. The building had not lacked capacity. It had lacked visible information about that capacity.

The staff learned an important difference between resources and access to resources. Empty seats are useful only if people know they exist and feel confident enough to look for them. Perfect information was not necessary. A simple estimate, clearly labeled as an estimate, was enough to help people make better choices. Sometimes congestion can be reduced not by creating more space, but by making existing space easier to understand.
translation:
市の学習センターには三つの階に自習室がありました。毎夕、一階の席を待つ列ができる一方、三階には空席が多く残っていました。職員は、利用者が入口に近い場所を好むのだと思い、一階に机を増やすことを検討しました。

しかし家具を買う前に調査すると、別の理由が分かりました。三階に空席があるかどうか分からないため、上まで行って満席だったら時間の無駄だと考え、目に見える一階の列に並ぶ人が多かったのです。実際には三階が満席になることはほとんどありませんでした。

高価な座席管理システムを導入する余裕はなかったため、もともと安全確認で巡回している職員が三十分ごとに各階のおおよその空席を記録し、入口の小さな掲示板に『空席多い』『少し空きあり』『ほぼ満席』と表示することにしました。正確な人数ではありませんが、判断には役立ちます。

最初の週には、利用者が表示を完全に正確な情報だと思ってしまう問題が起きました。『空席多い』と書かれていても直後に大人数が上がれば状況は変わります。そこで『最近の目安』と書き、確認時刻も表示しました。これだけで誤解が減りました。

一か月後、一階の列は特に平日の夕方に短くなり、三階の利用者が増えました。新しい机を買う計画も不要になりました。足りなかったのは席そのものではなく、席があることを示す情報だったのです。

職員は『資源があること』と『その資源を利用できること』は同じではないと学びました。空席があっても、存在を知らず探しに行く自信がなければ役立ちません。完璧な情報は必要なく、目安であることを明確にした簡単な表示だけで十分でした。混雑を減らすには、空間を増やすより、今ある空間を分かりやすくする方が効果的な場合があるのです。

title: The School Newspaper's Correction Box
passage:
The school newspaper at Koyo Junior High was published once a month. Students wrote articles about clubs, events, and interviews with teachers. The editors were proud of checking spelling carefully, but one issue contained a mistake in a sports article. A student's score was printed as 18 points instead of 8. The error was small, yet the student felt embarrassed because classmates kept asking about it.

The editors apologized and corrected the online version immediately. For the printed copies, however, the mistake could not be erased. At the next meeting, some editors argued that they should avoid drawing more attention to it. Others said that pretending the mistake had not happened would damage trust.

They decided to create a small ‘Corrections’ box in the next issue. It listed the wrong sentence, the correct information, and a short apology. The editors expected readers to see the box as a sign of failure. Instead, several teachers praised them for being clear about the mistake. One teacher explained that professional newspapers also publish corrections because accuracy includes fixing errors openly, not only trying to prevent them.

After that, the editors changed their process. Each article was checked by someone who had not written it, and numbers such as dates, scores, and prices were compared with the original notes. Even with the new system, another minor mistake appeared two months later. This time, the editors corrected it without a long debate.

The correction box gradually became a regular part of the newspaper, although many issues had nothing to put in it. Its empty presence still had meaning. It reminded the team that readers should be able to see when information changes.

The experience taught the editors that trust does not require pretending to be perfect. In fact, claiming perfect accuracy can make a later mistake more damaging. A trustworthy source does two things: it works carefully before publishing, and it responds clearly when something slips through. The students became less afraid of admitting errors, not because errors were unimportant, but because they had a fair method for repairing them.
translation:
光陽中学校の学校新聞は月に一度発行され、部活動や行事、先生へのインタビューなどを掲載していました。編集部は誤字を丁寧に確認していましたが、ある号のスポーツ記事で、生徒の得点を8点ではなく18点と印刷してしまいました。小さな誤りでしたが、本人は何度も聞かれて恥ずかしい思いをしました。

編集部は謝罪し、オンライン版はすぐ修正しました。しかし印刷済みの紙面は消せません。次の会議では、これ以上注目を集めない方がよいという意見と、間違いをなかったことにする方が信頼を損なうという意見に分かれました。

そこで次号に小さな『訂正』欄を作り、誤った文、正しい情報、短いお詫びを掲載しました。編集部は失敗の印だと思われることを心配しましたが、何人かの先生は明確に訂正したことを評価しました。プロの新聞でも訂正を出し、正確さとは間違いを防ぐだけでなく、起きた間違いを公開して直すことも含むと説明されました。

その後、記事は書いた本人以外が確認し、日付、得点、金額などの数字は元のメモと照合するようにしました。それでも二か月後に別の小さな誤りが出ましたが、今度は長い議論をせず訂正できました。

訂正欄は新聞の決まった場所になり、訂正がない号でも欄自体は残りました。空欄であることにも意味があり、情報が変わったとき読者が確認できる仕組みがあることを示していました。

編集部は、信頼されるために完璧なふりをする必要はないと学びました。むしろ完全無欠を主張すると、後の失敗がより大きな不信につながります。信頼できる情報源は、公開前に注意深く確認し、それでも漏れた誤りには明確に対応します。間違いが重要でないからではなく、公平に修正する方法を持ったことで、生徒たちは誤りを認めることを過度に恐れなくなりました。

title: The Park Gate That Stayed Open
passage:
A neighborhood park had two entrances. The main gate faced a busy street and stayed open from early morning until evening. A smaller side gate connected the park to a quiet residential area. For security reasons, the city planned to lock the side gate after six in the evening. The decision seemed reasonable because fewer people used it at night.

Before the change began, a residents' group asked the city to study who actually used the gate. Volunteers observed the entrance for one week. They found that the number of users after six was small, but many were older residents returning from a nearby supermarket. Closing the gate would add nearly ten minutes to their walk because they would have to go around the park to the main entrance.

The city still had concerns. A dark path near the side gate had received complaints, and staff wanted to reduce places where people could enter unnoticed. Instead of choosing only between ‘open’ and ‘locked,’ they tested a third option. The gate remained open until eight, and two solar lights were installed along the path. Bushes beside the entrance were trimmed so the area could be seen more clearly from nearby houses.

For six weeks, park staff recorded problems. No increase in damage or late-night gatherings was reported. Older residents said the route felt safer because the new lighting improved visibility. A few people asked why the gate could not remain open all night, but the city kept the eight o'clock closing time because the park itself officially closed then.

The discussion changed how the residents' group viewed usage numbers. If planners had looked only at the number of people using the gate after six, the group would have seemed too small to matter. But the effect of closure on each user was large. Ten extra minutes on a map may be minor for some people and difficult for others.

The final decision did not satisfy every preference, yet it balanced several needs better than the original plan. The group learned that public spaces should not be judged only by how many people use a feature. It can also matter who depends on it, what alternative they have, and how much a change would affect their daily routine.
translation:
近所の公園には二つの入口があり、正門は交通量の多い道路側、小さな脇門は住宅街側にありました。防犯上の理由から、市は利用者が少ない午後六時以降、脇門を施錠する計画を立てました。

しかし住民グループが利用状況を一週間調べると、六時以降の人数は少ないものの、その多くが近くのスーパーから帰る高齢者だと分かりました。門を閉めると公園を大きく回り、正門まで行く必要があるため、帰宅時間が約十分長くなります。

一方、市には暗い通路への苦情や、防犯上の心配がありました。そこで『開けるか閉めるか』だけで考えず、午後八時までは開けたままにし、通路に太陽光式ライトを二つ設置しました。入口周辺の茂みも低くして、近くの家から見通せるようにしました。

六週間、問題が起きないか記録しましたが、破損や夜間の集まりは増えませんでした。高齢者からは、照明が付いたことで以前より安全に感じるという声も出ました。終夜開放を求める声もありましたが、公園自体の閉園時間が八時なので、門もその時間に閉めることになりました。

この議論を通じ、住民は利用人数だけでは判断できないと気づきました。六時以降の利用者数だけ見れば少数ですが、その門が閉じたとき一人ひとりが受ける影響は大きかったからです。地図上の十分は、人によっては小さな差でも、別の人には大きな負担になります。

最終案は全員の希望を満たしたわけではありませんが、最初の計画より複数の必要をうまく両立しました。公共空間では『何人が使うか』だけでなく、『誰が頼っているか』『代わりの経路はあるか』『変更が日常にどれほど影響するか』も考える必要があるのです。

title: The Missing Ten Minutes
passage:
Mina joined an online English conversation group that met every Tuesday at seven. The session officially lasted one hour, but Mina noticed that actual speaking practice often began around 7:10. The first ten minutes were spent waiting for late members, checking microphones, and deciding who would speak first. Nobody considered the delay serious, yet over four meetings the group lost almost forty minutes of practice.

Mina did not want the meetings to feel strict or unfriendly. Several members joined after work or club activities, so occasional lateness was unavoidable. She suggested changing what happened at the beginning rather than telling everyone to arrive earlier.

The group created a five-minute ‘warm-up board.’ A short question was posted before each meeting, such as ‘What was one good thing about your day?’ Anyone who arrived on time could begin discussing it immediately in pairs. Late members could enter quietly and join the next pair without interrupting the whole group. Technical checks were also moved before the official start; members could enter the online room from 6:55 if they wanted to test sound.

The change did not make every meeting start perfectly. Sometimes the organizer had an internet problem, and once nearly everyone arrived late because of heavy rain. Still, most weeks speaking began within two or three minutes of seven. Members said the warm-up felt less like wasted waiting and more like an easy beginning.

After a month, the organizer estimated that the group had gained about half an hour of additional speaking time without extending any meeting. Mina found this result interesting because nothing had become faster. Nobody was asked to speak more quickly, and the official schedule did not change. The group simply changed how uncertain waiting time was used.

The experience made Mina notice similar ‘missing minutes’ elsewhere: students waiting for a teacher to connect a projector, people standing silently before a club meeting, or families deciding what to do while a meal finishes cooking. Not every short pause needs to be filled. Rest and waiting can be valuable. But when a group repeatedly loses time for the same reason, redesigning the beginning can sometimes recover useful minutes without making the schedule more demanding.
translation:
ミナは毎週火曜日の七時から、一時間のオンライン英会話グループに参加していました。しかし実際に会話練習が始まるのは7時10分ごろになることが多く、最初の十分は遅れてくる人を待ったり、マイクを確認したり、最初に話す人を決めたりしていました。一回ごとの遅れは小さく見えますが、四回で約四十分の練習時間が失われます。

ミナは、会を厳しくしたり、遅刻する人を責めたりしたくありませんでした。仕事や部活の後に参加する人もいるため、遅れることは避けられません。そこで『もっと早く来て』と言うのではなく、最初の時間の使い方を変えることを提案しました。

毎回、開始前に簡単な質問を掲示し、時間どおり来た人はすぐ二人組で話し始めることにしました。遅れた人は静かに入り、次の組み替えから参加できます。音声確認も開始前へ移し、希望者は6時55分から接続できるようにしました。

すべての会が完璧に始まるようになったわけではありません。主催者の通信障害が起きたり、大雨でほぼ全員が遅れたりした日もありました。それでも多くの週で、七時から二、三分以内に会話が始まりました。参加者は、ウォームアップが『待ち時間』ではなく自然な始まりに感じられると話しました。

一か月後、会の時間を延ばさずに約三十分多く話せたと推定されました。誰かが速く話すよう求められたわけでも、予定を長くしたわけでもありません。不確実な待ち時間の使い方を変えただけでした。

ミナはその後、プロジェクター接続を待つ授業、会議開始前に黙って待つ時間、料理ができるまで家族が何をするか迷う時間など、身の回りの『消える数分』にも気づくようになりました。短い待ち時間すべてを埋める必要はありません。休むことにも価値があります。しかし同じ理由で繰り返し時間を失うなら、始め方を設計し直すことで、負担を増やさず有効な時間を取り戻せる場合があります。
